title: Scaling Theory
intro: How shrinking a MOSFET changes its current, capacitance, speed and power, and why the same scaling that helps digital logic hurts analog dynamic range (Razavi, Section 17.1).

blocks.text: Dennard's ideal rules: divide every lateral and vertical dimension ($W$, $L$, $t_{ox}$, junction depth) and both $V_{DD}$ and $V_{TH}$ by $\alpha > 1$, and multiply every doping level by $\alpha$. Fields stay constant, hence the name.

blocks.alt: Cross-section of an NMOS transistor next to a copy half the size, with an arrow from the large to the small one.
blocks.caption: Ideal scaling shrinks everything, including the voltages.

blocks.text: The channel capacitance $WLC_{ox}$ falls by $\alpha$. Depletion widths shrink by $\alpha$ (doping up, voltage down, if $V_R \gg \phi_B$), so junction bottom capacitance per area rises by $\alpha$ while sidewall capacitance per length stays (the junction is shallower); with the areas and perimeters shrinking, every junction capacitance also falls by $\alpha$.

Gates get $\alpha$ times faster, density rises by $\alpha^2$, and the power per gate falls by $\alpha^3$ at the same clock, or by $\alpha^2$ if the clock rises by $\alpha$ (power density then unchanged). This is the engine behind Moore's observation that transistor counts double every year or two.

($\lambda$ rises by $\alpha$ because $\Delta L/L$ stays fixed while $V_{DS}$ shrinks.) So ideal scaling keeps $g_m$, $r_O$ and the intrinsic gain $g_mr_O$ constant; real processes have in fact lost intrinsic gain. The real blow is the supply: allowed swings shrink by $\alpha$, while thermal noise, set by $g_m$, does not. The dynamic range (maximum swing over noise) therefore falls by $\alpha$.

Restoring it requires noise voltages $\alpha$ times smaller, so $g_m$ must grow by $\alpha^2$ (noise voltage goes as $1/\sqrt{g_m}$). With the overdrive scaled down by $\alpha$, $g_m = 2I_D/V_{ov}$ forces $I_D$ up by $\alpha$, so power $(V_{DD}/\alpha)(\alpha I_D)$ stays constant, and $W$ must grow by $\alpha$ instead of shrinking, raising device capacitance by $\alpha$. If $kT/C$ noise sets the floor, keeping the slew rate costs even more current, and power rises.

Supplies and thresholds have not shrunk as fast as dimensions (for example $V_{DD}$ went from 5 V to 2.5 V and $V_{TH}$ from 0.8 V to 0.4 V while L went from 1 µm to 0.25 µm). Constant-voltage scaling, where dimensions shrink but voltages stay, raises every field by $\alpha$, risking breakdown and worsening short-channel effects. Actual technologies have followed a mix of the two, with device engineering to keep them reliable.

blocks.title: Scaling
blocks.text: Technology is scaled by $S = 1.4$. The old gate length is 180 nm. Find the new length, the relative gate delay, and the relative power per gate if the clock frequency also rises by $S$.
solution: Power per gate: $fCV^2 \to (Sf)(C/S)(V/S)^2 = P/S^2 = 0.51P$ (at a fixed clock it would be $1/S^3 = 0.36$).

blocks.title: Drain current after scaling
blocks.text: A transistor carrying 1 mA is ideally scaled by $\alpha = 2$ with its bias voltages. What current does it carry, and what happens to its $g_m$ and $r_O$?

blocks.title: Keeping the dynamic range
blocks.text: A thermal-noise-limited amplifier is moved to a process scaled by $\alpha = 2$ (supply halved). (a) By how much does its dynamic range fall if $g_m$ is kept? (b) To restore it, by what factors must $g_m$, $I_D$, $W$ and power change?
solution: (a) Swing halves, noise is unchanged: dynamic range falls by 2 (6 dB).
(b) Noise voltage must halve, so $g_m \times 4$. With $V_{ov}/2$, $I_D = g_mV_{ov}/2$ grows by 2. $W$ grows by 2 (instead of halving). Power $(V_{DD}/2)(2I_D)$ is unchanged.

blocks.title: Constant-voltage scaling
blocks.text: A 4 nm oxide carries 1.8 V. The process is scaled by 2 at constant voltage. Compare the oxide field before and after with a breakdown field of about 10 MV/cm.
solution: After: $1.8\text{ V}/2\text{ nm} = 9\text{ MV/cm}$, uncomfortably close to breakdown, which is why supplies had to come down.
